thread.title: These earnings are teaching investors a deeper lesson

author: Tim Mullaney
title: These earnings are teaching investors a deeper lesson
text:
Told you so!
Facebook’s FB, +10.08% first-quarter earnings report nicely exploded the hype about how the Cambridge Analytica “scandal” would lead to plagues, locusts, and a tidal wave of defections by Facebook and Instagram users and advertisers. Profit surged 63%, revenue jumped 49%, and once-troublesome metrics like slowing sales growth and a tiny bit of shrinkage in U.S. and Canadian usage of Facebook reversed themselves.
All you needed to do to see it coming was read some market research about how few people were actually deleting their Facebook accounts , which was widely available even as Facebook shares were slumping and as members of the House of Representatives and Senate were lining up to demonstrate equal amounts of outrage over, and ignorance of, how Facebook works, what data it collects and discloses, and how it makes money.
Put another way: Ted Cruz hasn’t been so completely pied in the face since former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates schooled him on the Constitution last May.
It did my heart a little good,
“Senator, They Run Ads… Lots of Them!,” wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Mark Mahaney in a note this morning.
Underneath the snark, and the small note of (admittedly interim) triumph at being right, there are a few serious points to make — all that should eventually work their way into Facebook’s stock price.
First, consumers react a lot less to privacy issues than elites do — probably because they understand the basic bargain they make with sites like Facebook.
Facebook’s business is based on what a marketing professor once described to me as “the second exchange:” The first exchange between a company and a consumer is cash payment for a good or service, and the second is some desired benefit in exchange for information about the consumer. In Facebook’s case, this means data about your Facebook posts and what you choose to put in your “public profile,’’ which journalists routinely describe as private data.
This exchange is basically how Mark Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg describe Facebook — a free service made possible by being able to sell targeted advertising. People get it, and they line up for it — 2.2 billion average monthly users last quarter, with 1.45 billion daily average users.
Read: Facebook says you are NOT the product — but its explanation confounds privacy experts
Even if Tesla’s TSLA, +0.57% Elon Musk and Apple’s AAPL, +0.13% Tim Cook disapprove of the second exchange, it passed the market test years ago, at both Facebook and Google GOOG, +2.11% GOOGL, +2.34% which have a combined market cap of $1.2 trillion.
Market tests should be heeded.
This is true partly because of the second much-overlooked truism: Most of the information Facebook has, and indirectly sells to advertisers, is not as intrusive as you’d guess from the prattling on about “selling your personal data.’’ So users don’t sweat it — and won’t begin sweating it soon.
I was one of many reporters who pulled my own Facebook history in response to this scandal, including info on which advertisers had requested information about me and what Facebook thought were my key interests based on what I’ve written on the site and who my friends are. I found about four advertiser requests a year for the decade I’ve been on Facebook. By contrast, I can get four telemarketing calls in a morning, and two months ago deleted 10,000 unread emails from Groupon alone.
The “data” was a fairly comical mishmash, not least because I took a few simple steps (like never giving Facebook my phone numbers, and putting a 1905 birth date in my profile) to make myself less attractive to advertisers. I also don’t answer many quizzes from Facebook’s app partners, one of whom was the source of all the data improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica, which advised Donald Trump’s presidential campaign. And when I do, I usually goof around with the answers to see if I can game the quiz’s conclusions about me.
Facebook, as a result, thinks I like cats, fiddle music and Republicans — a result of my posts about a standard poodle named Fiddle, plus a lot of whingeing about Trump that, as I recall, began with a 2015 debate-night observation that the future president was so incoherent I wanted to give him a quarter toward a tallboy out of sympathy. (Trump doesn’t drink, but as we were reminded as recently as Thursday morning’s Fox & Friends , he can ramble with the best drunks).
I’m less than overwhelmed, having read my own profile, by the prospect of my life being laid bare for all and sundry to see. That 1905 birth date spares me all manner of annoying age-targeted ads, so far without a corresponding surge of pitches from cemeteries.
If Facebook’s data is better than what advertisers have had to work with before — and that is a proposition that has also passed the market test — that’s OK. Its balance with privacy (at least mine) isn’t out of whack.
Read: How to disconnect the 25,000 malicious apps still stealing your Facebook data
That leads to a third conclusion: Investors shouldn’t worry much about new regulation of Facebook’s ad practices.
In the U.S., Facebook is confronted by an administration with the attention span of a flea, plus the ethics of Consumer Financial Protection Bureau chief Mick Mulvaney, who took time off his day job running the Office of Management and Budget to give a speech this week bragging that he only takes bank lobbyists’ calls if they make campaign contributions .
If I’m a Facebook investor, I’m lying awake nights wondering if Harvard dropout Mark Zuckerberg will be able to crack this crowd’s code. Short version: Send a check. Long game: Wait for them to be distracted by the next bonkers headline when the president opens his mouth.
But the real news is what Facebook said about Europe, which actually is tightening regulations on sharing user data with advertisers. It’s beginning to test procedures for how it will operate under the new rules, and finding little to no effect on user behavior .
Put it together, and that’s why Facebook is up more than 9% by midday Thursday. That trend will last longer than a good number of congressional careers.
